## Load packages and data

```{r load-packages, message = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(openintro)
```

## Exercises

### Exercise 1

According to the data dictionary, there are 52,519 pets in the dataset.

### Exercise 2

According to the data dictionary, there are 7 variables in the dataset.

### Exercise 3

The 3 most common pet names are Lucy, Charlie and Luna.

```{r popular-pet-names}
named_pets <- seattlepets %>% 
  filter(!is.na(animal_name))

named_pets %>%
  count(animal_name, sort = TRUE, name = "pet_number") %>%
  slice_max(pet_number, n=3)
```

### Exercise 4

The top 5 cat and dog names are as follows:

```{r most-common-cat-dog-names}
named_pets <- seattlepets %>% 
  filter(!is.na(animal_name))

named_pets %>%
   group_by(species) %>%
   count(animal_name, sort = TRUE, name = "pet_n") %>%
   slice_max(pet_n, n=5)
```

### Exercise 5

The animal names that are below the line are more common for cat than dogs: Oliver & Lili.

### Exercise 6

The relationship between the two variables (proportion of cats with a given name and proportion of dogs with a given name) is positive. In context of the data it means, that if a popularity of a cat name increases, the popularity of the dog name increases as well.
